lenses: logic, causal claims and the registers

findings.claim: Over this period gold behaved like the hedge in the definition and Bitcoin did not: it moved with stocks.
findings.evidence: Refuter: sensitivity and recompute outputs: gold's rolling 24-month r was positive in every window ending Jan 2022 to Sep 2024 (33 of 52). It exceeded the n = 24 5% critical value of 0.404 in 7 windows and was at or above Bitcoin's r in the windows ending 2023-03 and 2023-04 (recompute_out.txt). Gold's whole-period r = 0.164 has a Fisher 95% CI of [-0.065, 0.377], so a correlation as high as 0.38 is not excluded. Chart sh-4 shows the two lines overlapping from late 2022 to mid 2023. Adjudicator: I partly confirmed this (adj-stats/adj_out.txt). Gold's rolling 24-month r was positive in 33 of 52 windows, every window ending 2022-01 to 2024-09. It was above the n = 24 critical value of 0.404 in 7 windows, and at or above Bitcoin's r only in the windows ending 2023-03 and 2023-04. It was within 0.05 of Bitcoin's r in 7 windows (2022-11 to 2023-05), so the refuter's 'for about half of those windows ... about as much as Bitcoin' over-reaches. Whole-period gold r = 0.164 (Fisher 95% CI [-0.065, 0.377]) against Bitcoin's 0.515 [0.326, 0.664]. A Williams test on the two dependent correlations gives t = 2.42, p = 0.018, so the contrast with Bitcoin holds. Baur and Lucey define a hedge by the average relationship (sources/baur-lucey-2006...txt:115-116) and judge it by significance: 'the significance of the parameter estimates is the crucial number' (:548-549). Read against the whole-period average, the sentence follows the standard reading. What is real is the scope. 'Over this period' comes straight after the rolling-window sentence at md:85 and sits under chart sh-4. That chart's own title says gold's link 'came and went', and it shows gold tracking Bitcoin from late 2022 to mid 2023. So the sentence can be read as covering every window. This is scope precision, not a wrong fact
findings.fix: Narrow 'Over this period' to 'On average over the whole period'. This binds it to monthly.hedge.gold.p and monthly.hedge.bitcoin.p and to the definition's own 'on average' (md:36-37). The refuter's first fix is acceptable but cuts the link to the definition. The refuter's alternative, deleting 'gold behaved like the hedge in the definition and', leaves 'Over this period Bitcoin did not: it moved with stocks', which no longer parses.

findings.claim: It also got back to its starting level sooner in each: 55 trading days against 126, 505 against 513, and 51 against 89. ... Deeper falls, faster rebounds.
findings.evidence: Refuter: recompute2_out.txt: in 2022 Bitcoin first touched its 3 Jan 2022 level on 2024-01-08 (505 days), then closed 11.18% below it on 2024-01-18, the day before the S&P regained its high. sensitivity_out.txt, requiring 20 consecutive closes at or above the start: Bitcoin 528 days (2024-02-09) against S&P 513 (2024-01-19). In 2020 Bitcoin also fell back to 10.84% below its start on 2020-05-11, two trading days after its first touch, but it stays sooner on the persistence measure (110 against 181). Adjudicator: build_analysis.py:252-261 counts the first close at or above the start level, and the sh-3 footnote defines 'Back' the same way (make_charts.py:192-193). In 2022 Bitcoin first closed at or above its 3 Jan 2022 level on 2024-01-08 (505 days, +1.14%). It then fell to -11.18% on 2024-01-18 and -14.80% on 2024-01-22, while the S&P regained on 2024-01-19 (513 days) and stayed there (adj_out.txt). Bitcoin closed at or above the level only on 2024-01-08 and 2024-01-10, never on two days running, until 2024-02-09 (528 days). So any rule that needs even two consecutive closes reverses the 2022 order. 2020 (55 vs 126 first touch; 110 vs 181 with 20-day persistence) and 2025 (51 vs 89; 53 vs 89) hold either way. Two things soften it. The post already says 'In the 2022 episode they were close', and the chart footnote defines the measure. The claim also concedes a point to Bitcoin, and no verdict rests on it. So LOW, not MODERATE.
findings.fix: Narrow item 67 to 'It also first got back to its starting level sooner in each: ...', bound to episodes[*].*.regain_days and matching the sh-3 footnote. Deleting 'Deeper falls, faster rebounds.' is optional: once 'first' is in place, that line summarises the bound measure.

findings.claim: Bitcoin, gold and the S&P 500 as calendar-month averages, which dampen how deep a crash month looks.
findings.evidence: Refuter: checks3.py: the S&P's March 2020 change is -21.16% on monthly averages against -13.37% month-end to month-end. On aggregate the clause holds: the SD of averaged changes is 0.825 times the month-end SD, and the worst-8 mean is -7.41% against -8.42%. So averaging shrinks most crash months but deepened March 2020, the month without which the monthly Bitcoin verdict becomes 'cannot tell' (recompute_out.txt, drop 2020-03). Adjudicator: The sentence names no baseline. Measured against the daily path, averaging dampens March 2020 too. The S&P's fall from 19 Feb to 23 Mar 2020 is -41.44% log (34% simple, results.json episodes[0]), while the averaged March change is -21.16% log. The refuter's counterexample uses month-end changes. Averaging moves the late-February fall into March (Feb -0.03 averaged vs -8.79 month-end; Mar -21.16 vs -13.37). But February and March combined are -21.18 averaged vs -22.15 month-end, still shallower (adj3_out.txt). Across the sample, the SD ratio of 0.825 and the worst-8 mean of -7.41 vs -8.42 confirm dampening (adj_out.txt). The monthly Bitcoin verdict does not depend on it either. On month-end changes, Bitcoin's worst-10% interval is [-30.44, -2.35], still 'not a safe haven' (adj_out.txt). Design 8.2 (design.md:170) requires this caveat.

findings.claim: Bitcoin averaged minus 13.1 percent, with an interval from minus 24.8 to minus 1.4: not a safe haven. / Bitcoin is not a safe haven on monthly data with 2020 included
findings.evidence: Refuter: sensitivity_out.txt: the selected months are 2020-03, 2022-05/06, 2022-09/10, 2025-03/04 and 2026-03. Bitcoin's monthly-change lag-1 autocorrelation is 0.395; a simulated averaged random walk gives 0.23. Design effect 1.296 gives an adjusted interval of [-26.38, +0.22], which contains 0 and the S&P mean of -7.41. Keeping only non-adjacent months (n = 5) gives [-33.35, +1.13]. An iid bootstrap still gives [-22.21, -4.09]. The verdict is method-dependent (PLAUSIBLE). Gold stays 'weak' under all of these. Adjudicator: The selected months (adj2_out.txt) are 2020-03, 2022-05/06, 2022-09/10, 2025-03/04 and 2026-03, which is three adjacent pairs. Bitcoin's monthly-average changes have lag-1 autocorrelation 0.395 (SE about 0.115), and 0.394 after removing the S&P. On month-end prices it is 0.117, so the dependence comes mostly from the averaging. A design effect of 1 + 2*3*0.395/8 = 1.296 gives [-26.38, +0.22], which would be 'cannot tell'. With rho = 0.25, the averaging effect alone, the upper bound is about -0.35 and the verdict stands. The t-test gives p = 0.033 (adj3_out.txt), Wilcoxon signed-rank p = 0.078, and the sign test 2 of 8 up, p = 0.29. So the verdict sits on the boundary and depends on the method (PLAUSIBLE). Two things soften it. md:65 already says 'Eight months is a small sample' and that the monthly Bitcoin verdict rests on the Covid crash. Bitcoin's main verdict is the daily one (81 days, CI [-5.9, -2.8]). Gold stays weak under every variant.
findings.fix: Narrow md:63 'not a safe haven' to 'not a safe haven by my test', matching the gold clause in the same paragraph. md:143 sits under 'Scored conditions', which already reports scoring against the pre-registered test. Narrowing it the same way is the owner's call.

findings.claim: FRED allows non-commercial educational or personal use with the notice kept

FRED's rule for exactly that category, fred_legal_notices.txt:199, says such series 'may only be used for non-commercial educational or personal use' without the holder's written permission. The data README paraphrases the provision specific to this series accurately, and it also states S&P's copyright. FAQ :129 and ToU :271 are FRED's more general and stricter wording, so FRED's own pages conflict; citing the specific provision is not a misstatement. Deleting the clause would not change the real exposure. The residual risk is S&P's own notice ('Reproduction of S&P 500 in any form is prohibited', series page :204), which only S&P Dow Jones Indices can waive (index_services@spdji.com, :206). The owner should know this, but no README edit settles it.
